Five-part treatment applied to every subsystem

This edition preserves the CAM manuscript's five-part treatment for every load-bearing subsystem:

  1. Why it exists — the specific failure mode this subsystem prevents, described with a scenario a junior developer can visualize.
  2. What it is responsible for — the one-sentence contract, plus an exhaustive list of side effects.
  3. How it hands off — the exact data type flowing out, the exact call site that consumes it, and the invariant that must hold.
  4. Alternatives considered — the alternatives that were considered and rejected, and why.
  5. Where the idea came from — because a mechanism that reads as arbitrary in isolation reads as inevitable the moment you see the reason it was chosen.

How to read this at your level

The Arabic manuscript established a four-tier reading map that this edition preserves:

  • Junior developers should read every paragraph, skipping only the "PhD note" boxes on first pass.
  • Senior developers can skim the foundational paragraphs and dwell on the mechanism paragraphs.
  • Master-level readers should focus on the "trade-offs considered" and "failure modes" sections.
  • PhD readers should use the PhD notes as shortcuts into the calibration and statistical-guarantee content.

Part 0 — The distributed-cognition thesis

This part is condensed from the CAM manuscript's Part 0. It is the philosophical framing of the project. The engineering reference in Parts 1–8 implements the ideas laid out here.

0.1   The traditional assumption

Most AI systems, one way or another, assume something like this: the model itself is expected to carry almost everything — knowledge, reasoning, planning, decomposition, self-criticism, error detection, correction, and the final judgment. And when the model is wrong, we typically tell it “think again” or “review your answer.” But in the end the same model is the one being asked to discover its own error.

0.2   ClaudeDeep starts from a different assumption

ClaudeDeep treats the model as a component inside a larger reasoning architecture. The model does not have to be perfect. It only needs to be capable enough to: 

understand the task
perform reasonable reasoning
follow a specialized reasoning procedure
read the evidence
emit structured JSON
call functions
understand verification results
and revise its output

The architecture carries the rest of the load.

0.3   What the architecture externalizes

Everything the traditional single-model design keeps implicit inside the weights is, in ClaudeDeep, explicitly represented as a subsystem in the architecture: 

Knowledge  ->  GraphRAG substrate  (corpus + graph + trust tiers)
Reasoning policy  ->  Skills + ModuleFAQ (per-module assertions)
Failure knowledge  ->  RejectedChunkLog + FAQ probes
Adversarial verification  ->  Builder vs Saboteur, at 4 layers
Correction  ->  iterative recursion with 3 halt conditions
Verification  ->  conformal calibration + Z3-SMT gate
The contract  ->  Pydantic-enforced 100%-or-abstain type union
Verified against code: The classes named above exist in the codebase. GraphRAGEngine, Builder, Saboteur, ModuleFAQ, ConfidenceScore, ConformalCalibrator, SMTVerifier, AbstentionReport, AnswerReport. Every one grep-checked in src/claudedeep/.

0.4   Builder and Saboteur — the adversarial primitive

This is one of the strongest primitives in ClaudeDeep. The Saboteur is not there to say “I disagree.” It is there to say “try to prove this candidate is wrong.” That changes the nature of the reasoning:

  • The Builder asks: “How do I construct a good solution?”
  • The Saboteur asks: “How do I break this solution?”

That is closer to adversarial verification than to mere debate. And because the Builder retrieves Supporting evidence while the Saboteur retrieves Counter evidence, retrieval itself becomes role-aware.

0.5   Even agreement doesn’t mean the answer is correct

Suppose the Builder says “correct” and the Saboteur also says “correct.” Are we done? Not necessarily. Both may have relied on the same wrong evidence. If there is a large correlation between their sources, ClaudeDeep treats it as a risk and reruns the Saboteur with more independent sources.

Verified against code (Q-Fix.H): src/claudedeep/agents/module_agent.py measures the Jaccard overlap between Builder chunk_ids and Saboteur chunk_ids and, when the overlap exceeds 0.5, reruns the Saboteur with an excluded_chunk_ids filter equal to the Builder’s set. Retries are capped at 8. This puts the system closer to independence-aware verification than to simple multi-agent voting.

0.6   Phase 1 and Phase 2 — the module boundary

Modules can be individually correct but wrong when integrated: 

Module A = correct
Module B = correct
does NOT imply:
A + B = correct

ClaudeDeep separates the two questions:

  • Phase 1: is this module itself correct?
  • Phase 2: do these modules operate together correctly?

That distinction matters especially in Software Engineering, where the biggest problems typically aren’t in a single component — they are in the interaction between components. And when Phase 2 discovers such a problem, it can loop back to decomposition with a FullContext rather than ignoring the incompatibility.

0.7   The loops are where the leverage is

The primary model might produce an imperfect first attempt. ClaudeDeep is not obliged to accept the result. It can: 

First Attempt
    -> Counter Evidence
    -> Saboteur Attack
    -> Failure
    -> Failure Analysis
    -> Rebuild
    -> Attack Again
    -> Verify

You are not asking the model for perfect first-pass reasoning. You are building iterative reasoning + error correction on top of a model that only needs to clear a modest capability threshold.

0.8   Cognition moves from weights into the system

If you want to summarize the whole architecture in one point: traditional systems put knowledge, reasoning, criticism, memory, verification, and correction largely inside the model. ClaudeDeep distributes them across independent subsystems. That is the architectural heart of the project.

0.9   The thesis in one sentence

ClaudeDeep does not attempt to make a mid-tier model behave like a frontier model in a single pass; it builds a reasoning environment that enables a mid-tier model to construct, attack its own construction, use evidence, detect failure, rebuild, verify, and integrate results — until the system arrives at a defensible outcome.
Bridge to Part 1: Part 0 has said what ClaudeDeep is trying to be. Part 1 sets the empirical context in which it operates — where frontier LLMs are in May 2026, what they lack, and why the 100%-or-abstain framing is the right answer to those specific gaps.

Part 1 — The landscape of reasoning LLMs in May 2026

Every design decision in ClaudeDeep is a response to something the frontier does or does not do. This part establishes the empirical baseline. Everything after it is justified against these numbers.

1.1   What the frontier can do today

As of May 2026, three closed-weight model families lead the public reasoning benchmarks. The canonical yardstick for practical software-engineering ability — SWE-bench Verified, a 500-instance subset of real GitHub issues on which the model must produce a patch that passes the hidden tests without ever seeing them — sits at the following levels:

ModelVendorSWE-bench Verified pass@1Weights
Claude Mythos PreviewAnthropic93.9%Closed
Claude Opus 4.7 (Adaptive)Anthropic87.6%Closed
GPT-5.3 CodexOpenAI85.0%Closed
Claude Opus 4.5Anthropic80.9%Closed
InfCode (agent scaffold on DeepSeek-V3 / Claude 4.5 Sonnet)Research (arxiv 2511.16004)79.4%Scaffold open, base closed
GLM-5 (~70B)Zhipu77.8%Open
Best published 7B model, raw pass@1Various< 15% (never above 40% in ANY published scaffold)Open
Junior orientation. "pass@1" means the model was given one attempt per problem and the patch either passes all hidden tests or does not. No retries, no oracle, no human intervention. 93.9% means the model solved 469 of 500 problems on the first attempt.

Every model above 77% has one thing in common: it is either closed-weight, or far larger than 7B parameters, or both. Closed weights mean the user must send their code to an external API. Large weights mean the user needs multi-GPU inference infrastructure — for a 70B model at FP16, roughly 140 GB of VRAM, the territory of two A100 80GB cards.

This is the empirical wall ClaudeDeep's hypothesis pushes against. The hypothesis is not “a 7B can match Mythos on raw pass@1”. No public architecture has closed that gap. The hypothesis is narrower and more defensible: a 7B–20B-class model wrapped in the right scaffolding — real retrieval over a canonical CS corpus, adversarial verification at every layer, conformal-calibrated abstention — can produce ANSWERS at ≥ 99% precision on the subset of queries it doesn’t abstain on. Raw coverage may be modest, but every emitted answer carries a traceable, verifier-corroborated evidence chain.

1.2   The four gaps ClaudeDeep is built to close

Frontier LLMs in their default deployment have four architectural gaps. Each is the justification for a specific ClaudeDeep subsystem. Understanding the gap is a prerequisite for understanding why the corresponding subsystem exists at all.

1.2.1   Gap 1 — no abstention contract

Mythos scores 93.9% on Verified. The remaining 6.1% is not “the model told the user I don’t know.” It is the model emitting a confident-looking patch that broke the hidden tests, with nothing in the response suggesting the answer might be wrong. Run Mythos against 10,000 real GitHub issues and roughly 610 of them receive a plausible-but-broken patch that, at the response level, is indistinguishable from the 9,390 correct answers.

For low-stakes contexts this is acceptable — a human reviewer catches the bad patches. For high-stakes contexts (medical decision support, legal document analysis, infrastructure configuration) it is a catastrophe. A wrong answer at 94% confidence is worse than no answer, because the user acts on the wrong answer.

ClaudeDeep’s response. Phase3 emits either an AnswerReport or an AbstentionReport — mutually exclusive Pydantic types enforced at the type-system level. The choice depends on an aggregated confidence score computed from three orthogonal signals: (a) the agreement fraction of the winning cluster in best-of-N sampling, (b) the Process Reward Model score, (c) the conformal-calibrated threshold derived from a held-out eval set. Every abstention carries a typed reason.

Verified against code. The seven typed AbstentionReason values, defined at src/claudedeep/a2a/messages.py:353, are: corpus_gap, unsat_core, recursion_cap, adversarial_rejection, execution_unachievable, proof_incomplete, cross_mode_divergence. No "unknown" reason exists.

1.2.2   Gap 2 — no contract-first decomposition

Most agent scaffolds decompose a task implicitly during a single chain-of-thought pass, and discover module-boundary incompatibilities at runtime. When Module A’s plan needs an API that Module B’s plan does not provide, the scaffolds typically resolve this by having an LLM judge look at both plans and rewrite one of them. This is the override cascade: an LLM without grounding is given authority to overwrite peer decisions, and once that happens, the confidence chain becomes unreliable because you cannot trace which module’s plan is “the real one.”

ClaudeDeep’s response. Phase 0 emits N ModuleSpecs, each bound to a draft ContractBroadcast, before any Builder writes a single line of a plan. The contract contains the API schema, the event contracts, the data types, and the dependencies. Modules build within their contracts; they never renegotiate them. Residual conflicts in Phase 2 are resolved through deterministic arbiters — a CSP solver, then a Builder-vs-Saboteur clash on solver-generated candidates, then the user, then a re-decomposition — never by an LLM overwriting a peer.

Verified against code. class MasterOrchestrator in src/claudedeep/orchestrator/master.py emits OrchestrationPlan(module_specs, dependency_graph, faqs). class KCandidateDecomposer in src/claudedeep/orchestrator/k_candidate_decomposer.py generates the K=8 candidate decompositions when policy.k_candidate_decomposition=True. The classes HeuristicCandidateScorer and AdversarialCandidateScorer both exist and are stacked.

1.2.3   Gap 3 — no adversarial verification at every layer

Multi-agent debate systems perform adversarial verification at the output layer: an arbiter sees multiple candidate answers and picks one. InfCode adds adversarial verification at the test/patch layer for SWE-bench: a generator proposes a patch, a critic proposes a failing test, and if the test holds against the patch, both are accepted. Neither approach builds adversarial verification into every retrieval, plan synthesis, ingestion, and committed contract.

ClaudeDeep’s response — adversarial clash at four layers:

  • Phase 0 (decomposition): the Saboteur attacks each candidate decomposition draft, breaking its capability manifold and exposing missing dependencies.
  • Phase 1 (per-module plan): the classic Builder↔Saboteur clash. The Builder proposes a plan grounded in Supporting evidence; the Saboteur attacks with Counter evidence. The plan survives if no FAQ item is broken; otherwise it recurses with enriched context.
  • Phase 2 tier 3 (solver candidates): when tier 2’s CSP solver returns multiple SAT candidates, the Builder picks one, the Saboteur attacks it, and only the surviving candidate is committed.
  • Gap Resolver ingestion: the MultiPassSaboteur applies five attack families (injection, noise, duplicate, bias, contradiction) to every retrieved chunk before promotion. Rejected chunks are logged as counter-examples for future Saboteur runs.
Verified against code. Files src/claudedeep/agents/builder.py (class Builder), src/claudedeep/agents/saboteur.py (class Saboteur), src/claudedeep/clash/adversarial_clash.py (class AdversarialClash), src/claudedeep/gap_resolver/multi_pass_saboteur.py (class MultiPassSaboteur). All grep-confirmed.

1.2.4   Gap 4 — no 100%-or-abstain invariant

Selective-prediction and conformal-abstention research have converged on the same result: when a model is forced to choose between answering and abstaining at a calibrated threshold, the false-answer rate can be driven below 1% at 50–70% coverage. But this only works when the threshold is COMMITTED — a calibrated tau computed from a held-out set, not a heuristic. Most production systems default to a fixed confidence cutoff (typically 0.85) that nobody has actually calibrated against the true precision they care about.

ClaudeDeep’s response. Phase3 supports a ConformalCalibrator: point policy.conformal_calibration_path at a JSON file of (confidence, was_correct) pairs from a held-out eval set; the smallest tau achieving precision ≥ 1−ε is computed on load and replaces the heuristic 0.85. An empty calibration file preserves the heuristic (the “never worsen the baseline” invariant).

Verified against code. src/claudedeep/pipelines/conformal.py defines classes ConformalCalibrator, CalibrationDatum, and CalibrationResult. Policy field conformal_calibration_path: str | None = None at src/claudedeep/mode/policy.py. Policy field conformal_epsilon: float = 0.01 (the default 1% target false-answer rate).

1.3   The 7B equalizer thesis, in numbers

Why bother building a complex scaffold for a 7B-class open-weight model when frontier closed-weight LLMs already exist? Three reasons:

  • Sovereignty. A 7B Ollama model runs locally on a 16 GB GPU. Mythos requires Anthropic’s API. Opus requires Anthropic’s API. GPT-5.3 requires OpenAI’s API. For research labs, government contracts, regulated industries, and corpus owners who cannot send proprietary data over a vendor API, an open-weight self-hosted stack is the only option that exists.
  • Auditability. Every step in ClaudeDeep emits a structured TelemetryEvent. Every retrieval is logged with its CompiledQuery. Every Saboteur attack is replayable from its retrieval state. Every abstention carries a typed reason and an evidence chain. The same artifact ships to peer reviewers and to on-call debuggers.
  • Falsifiability. “A 7B with this scaffold reaches X% on SWE-bench Verified” is a testable claim. The realistic first-year target is 35–55%, and the 100%-or-abstain invariant means precision-on-answered should hit 99% regardless of coverage. Both are measurable.
Verified against code. class TelemetryEvent at src/claudedeep/observability/telemetry.py; four sink classes NullSink, SqliteSink, plus JSONL and in-memory implementations. class Replay and class ReplayCase at src/claudedeep/observability/replay.py. class ConfidenceChainRecorder at src/claudedeep/observability/confidence_chain.py.

1.4   What "beats Mythos" actually means here

The book is explicit about what "beats Mythos" means. It does NOT mean raw pass-rate parity on SWE-bench Verified — that is beyond current published evidence at any open-weight model size. It means precision-on-answered parity at lower coverage: where Mythos answers everything at 93.9%, ClaudeDeep answers roughly 50% at > 99% — each answer carries a traceable evidence chain, a calibrated confidence number, and a guaranteed precision floor. For high-stakes domains, precision IS the value; the coverage gap is the explicit trade.

The unfair-comparison disclaimer. When we say “beats Mythos on precision-on-answered,” we mean under a fixed conformal-calibration eval in which both systems are forced to abstain. Mythos’s published 93.9% is its answer rate; what fraction would survive a 99%-precision abstention filter is an open empirical question. ClaudeDeep is BUILT to deliver that filter; whether Mythos has one in its private deployment is unknown.

1.5   Reasoning as a system property (from CAM)

Sections 1.1–1.4 justified ClaudeDeep gap by gap, against specific frontier shortcomings. This section makes the same argument in reverse: not what the frontier is missing, but what a reasoning system needs to do, and why any reasoning system needs an architecture that turns the things the frontier conflates into a single place into distributed responsibilities that operate together.

In the traditional design, the model is expected to carry almost everything: domain knowledge, reasoning policy, decomposition, error detection, self-criticism, contradiction detection, correction, final judgment. When the model is wrong we ask it to think again — but the same model is being asked to detect its own error.

ClaudeDeep does not ask the primary model to carry the whole chain. It asks the model to clear a specific, bounded capability threshold — understand the task, perform a reasoning step, follow a specialized reasoning procedure, read evidence, emit structured JSON, call functions, understand verification results, revise its output. The architecture holds the rest of the chain: task decomposition, reasoning policies, knowledge grounding, adversarial challenge, counter-evidence, error discovery, verification, correction, integration, final decision.

That reframing is what makes a 7B–20B-class primary model viable as the substrate for an architecture that is larger than the model itself.

Part 2 — The pipeline, phase by phase, connection by connection

Part 1 explained why the system exists. Part 2 explains how it runs, from the moment the user types a request to the moment an AnswerReport or AbstentionReport leaves the outer loop. Every module gets the five-part treatment. Where a module is trivial, the parts collapse into a paragraph; where it is load-bearing, they are broken out explicitly.

2.0   Conventions

Two invariants restated up front

  • LLM = syntax compiler. Every LLM call passes through a ConstrainedDecoder (the concrete production class is OllamaConstrainedDecoder) with a Pydantic schema. There is no free-form text generation anywhere in the pipeline. Any module that tries to bypass this raises a ConstrainedDecoderError.
  • Recursion is Phase 1 only; pipeline recursion is main.py’s. Phase 1’s child-of-child recursion stays inside a module. Phase 2 tier 5 can emit a PipelineRecursionRequest to Phase 0 — but the decision to consume it is owned by main.py’s outer loop.
Verified against code. class ConstrainedDecoder, class OllamaConstrainedDecoder, class StubConstrainedDecoder, and class ConstrainedDecoderError at src/claudedeep/llm/constrained_decoding.py. class PipelineRecursionRequest and class FullContext at src/claudedeep/a2a/messages.py.

2.1   Phase 0 — Contract-first orchestration

Why it exists

Most agent scaffolds skip Phase 0. They accept a request, ask an LLM to think about how to approach it, and let the resulting free-form plan drive downstream modules. This works until modules need to interoperate — at which point an LLM judge is asked to reconcile them (the override cascade Gap 2 warned about) or the system breaks. Phase 0 exists to make module boundaries a contract, not an emergent property.

What it is responsible for

The MasterOrchestrator is a pure planner. Three side effects, in order: (1) issue a Phase-0-only ArchitecturalQuery against GraphRAG to fetch high-level architectural patterns; (2) hand the request and context to KCandidateDecomposer, which generates K=8 variant decompositions; (3) hand the K candidates to the stacked scorer, pick the winner, and call EffortAssigner to attach a per-module effort_level.

Verified against code. src/claudedeep/graphrag/queries.py defines exactly four query subclasses of GraphRAGQuery: SupportingQuery (line 41), CounterQuery (line 45), IntegrationQuery (line 49), ArchitecturalQuery (line 56). The type system forbids the wrong caller from constructing the wrong subtype. class Decomposer and class EffortAssigner at src/claudedeep/orchestrator/.

K=8 candidate decompositions (Q-Fix.G)

Instead of trusting a single decomposition draft, ClaudeDeep generates 8 structurally-diverse variants and scores each. The K generators are hard-coded strategies, not 8 samples from the same model with the same prompt — because K samples from the same model are correlated, and correlated candidates defeat the point of scoring K of them.

Each candidate is scored by AdversarialCandidateScorer stacked on HeuristicCandidateScorer: the heuristic scorer does structural checks with no LLM cost (dependency-graph validity, capability-manifold breadth, module-count penalty); the adversarial scorer runs one Builder/ Saboteur clash per module against each draft contract. The winner is the candidate that scores highest on the equal-weight combination.

Reconciled against code (default vs. overlay). The scorers exist and are stacked, but policy.k_candidate_decomposition defaults to False and policy.k_candidate_adversarial_scoring defaults to False. Both are turned on only under the quality-max overlay. The CAM manuscript describes them as always-on; that is the overlay behavior, not the code default.

How Phase 0 hands off

«MasterOrchestrator.plan(user_input, full_context)» → OrchestrationPlan(module_specs, dependency_graph, faqs) → «Phase1.run(...)». The OrchestrationPlan is frozen at construction; neither Phase 1 nor Phase 2 mutates it.

2.2   Phase 1 — Per-module adversarial resolution

Why it exists

Every module produced by Phase 0 is a plan, not a correct plan. Phase 1 turns each spec into a battle-tested plan via an adversarial cycle: the Builder proposes, the Saboteur attacks, the clash decides. If any attack breaks a FAQ item, the plan recurses with enriched context. Recursion continues until the plan survives, a convergence halt fires, or the recursion depth cap is hit — in which case Phase 1 emits ContractUnimplementable rather than falsely reporting success.

Verified against code. class ModuleAgent at src/claudedeep/agents/module_agent.py; class Phase1 and class Phase1Result at src/claudedeep/phases/phase1_resolution.py; class ContractUnimplementable and class SurvivedReport at src/claudedeep/a2a/messages.py.

The Builder is a five-stage pipeline, not an LLM writing a plan

The biggest misunderstanding of the Builder is that it is “an LLM that writes a plan.” No. The Builder is a five-stage pipeline where the LLM is the last stage. Every earlier stage constrains what the LLM can even see, reducing its job to “fill in the syntactic slots of a plan schema, given already-vetted evidence.”

  1. FAQ Validate. Load the module’s ModuleFAQ (from faqs/modules/<type>.yaml). Every FAQ item is a natural-language assertion the plan must satisfy. This is the input contract the Saboteur will later probe.
  2. CompiledQuery construction. Build a QueryIntent and pass it to the deterministic compile(), which returns a CompiledQuery(vector_q, graph_pattern, filters). This is the only entry point to GraphRAGEngine.query_compiled().
  3. GraphRAG Supporting query. Execute the compiled query through the hybrid retrieval stack. Returns list[GraphRAGHit], each with score, text, chunk_id, and provenance.
  4. Reranker (helpful stance). Prefer canonical, recent, corroborated evidence — provenance tier B or higher.
  5. LLMStage. The LLM finally enters. It receives a VerifiedContext(system_prompt, faq_snippet, graphrag_evidence) and returns LLMResult[Plan].
Verified against code. class Builder and class BuilderOutput at src/claudedeep/agents/builder.py. The four-stage primitives exist as separate files: pipelines/faq_validate.py (class ... via faq_validate), pipelines/faq_probe.py, pipelines/reranker.py (class Reranker), pipelines/llm_stage.py (class LLMStage, class VerifiedContext, class LLMResult). class CompiledQuery and class QueryIntent at src/claudedeep/graphrag/query_dsl.py.

The Saboteur is the same pipeline, Counter stance

The Saboteur runs the same five stages with three substitutions: (1) FAQ Validate becomes FAQ Probe (generate an attack angle for each FAQ item); (2) the QueryIntent.intent becomes "counter" with anti_patterns=true, so the compiled query pulls anti-patterns and failure modes; (3) the reranker uses a “damaging stance,” preferring chunks that contradict the Builder’s plan. Stage 5 emits LLMResult[SabotageResponse] whose payload contains attack_findings, broken_faq_items, and repair_recommendations.

AdversarialClash

The clash primitive is deliberately trivial: a plan survives iff len(broken_faq_items) == 0. Any broken item forces recursion. All intelligence lives in the FAQ Probe and the LLM’s per-attack finding; the clash exists as a named function only so telemetry and the recursion controller can inspect the sequence of decisions.

Verified against code. class AdversarialClash and class ClashOutcome at src/claudedeep/clash/adversarial_clash.py; class SabotageRequest, class SabotageResponse, class AttackFinding at src/claudedeep/a2a/messages.py.

RecursionController — three halt conditions

On a recurse decision, the controller decides whether to spawn a child or halt. Three halts, checked in order: (1) Depth cap — current depth ≥ max_pipeline_recursion; (2) Convergence delta — the count of broken FAQ items did not strictly decrease compared to the previous round; (3) Oscillation signature — the exact frozenset(broken_faq_items) has appeared at any prior round, detecting A→B→A→B cycles. On any halt, the module emits ContractUnimplementable.

Verified against code. class RecursionController and class HaltVerdict at src/claudedeep/clash/recursion_controller.py. Policy fields convergence_epsilon: int = 1 and convergence_max_repeats: int = 3 at src/claudedeep/mode/policy.py.

Phase 1 output — a typed union

Every ModuleAgent emits exactly one of: Phase1Result(status="SURVIVED", plan, confidence, evidence) or Phase1Result(status="CONTRACT_UNIMPLEMENTABLE", contract_unimplementable). The third status "FAILED" is reserved for infrastructure errors, distinct from a contract-level refusal after exhaustive attempts.

2.3   Phase 2 — The deterministic-arbiter cascade

Why every arbiter is deterministic

Phase 2 resolves inter-module conflicts — modules that individually passed their clash but whose contracts do not compose. The tempting design is an LLM judge that picks one of the conflicting contracts. That is the override cascade Gap 2 refused. Instead, Phase 2 resolves conflicts through a tier cascade where every arbiter is either deterministic (checker, solver) or a Builder/Saboteur clash operating on solver-generated candidates.

Verified against code. The six tier names, defined at src/claudedeep/a2a/messages.py:256 as TierName = Literal["conformance", "solver", "proofing", "clash", "ask_user", "re_decompose"]. The CAM manuscript numbers them 1, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5; the code names them. Note that proofing is a first-class tier between solver and clash (Phase M.3), not an afterthought. class A2ALayer2Hub at src/claudedeep/a2a/layer2_hub.py; class Phase2 and class Phase2Result at src/claudedeep/phases/phase2_conflict.py; class TierResult and the type alias ProofingVerdict = Literal["accept", "reject", "bypass"] in messages.py.

The six tiers

  • conformance. Deterministic pass: does every survived plan conform to its Phase-0 contract? If yes and no cross-module conflicts, the cascade halts and commits.
  • solver. A CSP solver over the modules’ capability manifolds. policy.solver_backend selects cp-sat (Google OR-Tools) or z3 (Microsoft). SAT with one candidate commits; SAT with multiple goes to the clash tier; UNSAT goes to the clash tier with a human-readable core.
  • proofing. When the solver returns SAT, the committed contract is checked against MCP-backed web search for counter-evidence. On reject, the SAT is demoted to a clash. On accept, new sources are ingested as tier-B provisional evidence.
  • clash. Builder vs Saboteur over the top-K solver-generated candidates. The Builder picks; the Saboteur attacks; the surviving candidate commits. Critical property: this tier never lets the LLM invent a new solution; it picks among candidates the solver already proved feasible.
  • ask_user. A bounded interaction: the request presents the plans, conflict summary, UNSAT core, attack findings, and a pre-generated option set. The user picks one or declines.
  • re_decompose. Structural retreat. Emit a PipelineRecursionRequest carrying a FullContext. The request returns to main.py, which decides whether to re-enter Phase 0 or, at the cap, force AbstentionReport(reason="recursion_cap").
Verified against code (solver backends). SolverBackend = Literal["cp-sat", "z3"] at src/claudedeep/mode/policy.py; default solver_backend: SolverBackend = "cp-sat"; solver_timeout_ms: int = 10000. Proofing: class ProofingVerifier, class ProofingResult, class StubProofingVerifier at src/claudedeep/proofing/verifier.py.

2.4   Phase 3 — Aggregation + 100%-or-abstain

Why the invariant is Pydantic-enforced

The 100%-or-abstain contract is exposed at the type-system level: Phase3Result is either an AnswerReport or an AbstentionReport. The two types are structurally incompatible; a Phase 3 code path that wants to return both cannot be written without a Pydantic error. This is what converts the invariant from a promise into a compile-time guarantee.

The pipeline into abstention

Given the survived modules, Phase3 aggregates their evidence chains, computes an aggregate confidence, and compares it against tau (the conformal-derived threshold, or the heuristic 0.85 if no calibration file is present). If confidence ≥ tau AND at least one tier-A/B evidence link exists, an AnswerReport is assembled. Otherwise the pipeline consults the cloud teacher, runs the Z3-SMT gate on any code-artifact invariants, and emits an AbstentionReport with a typed reason.

Verified against code. class Phase3 and class Phase3Result at src/claudedeep/phases/phase3_aggregation.py (the actual AbstentionReport(...) construction is at line 458). class SMTVerifier, class SMTVerification, class UnsatCore, class SMTConstraint, class SMTDeclaration, class SMTBackendUnavailable at src/claudedeep/pipelines/smt_verifier.py.

The seven typed abstention reasons

ReasonTrigger
corpus_gapAggregate confidence < tau, gap iterations exhausted
unsat_coreZ3 proved contract invariants unsatisfiable
recursion_capPhase 2 re_decompose emitted a recursion request at cap depth
adversarial_rejectionEvery generated candidate failed the clash
execution_unachievableExecution-mode rebuild-loop cap hit without passing tests
proof_incompleteZ3 timeout AND policy requires SMT
cross_mode_divergenceCross-mode validation found conflicting answers between modes
Verified against code. Exactly these seven values, in this order, at src/claudedeep/a2a/messages.py:353–361. There is no eighth reason and no "unknown".

2.5   The outer loop — main.py

main.py:run(user_input, root) wraps the four-phase flow in a bounded while loop that owns: (1) the fast-path classifier + answer cache (cache-hit returns immediately); (2) the clarification gate (ambiguous requests trigger a bounded question); (3) the pipeline-recursion budget (max_pipeline_recursion, default 3); (4) the gap-iteration budget (max_gap_iterations, default 3). At either cap the abstention becomes final.

Why bounded, not unbounded? The plan commits to “no latency budget” (individual LLM calls can be arbitrarily long) but not to “no recursion budget.” An unbounded outer loop is not “quality over latency” — it is “no termination guarantee,” which is a correctness bug. The bounded loop guarantees termination while allowing arbitrary inner compute.

Verified against code. class FastPathClassifier at src/claudedeep/fast_path/classifier.py; class QueryCache at src/claudedeep/fast_path/cache.py; class ClarificationGate, class ClarificationVerdict, class ClarificationQuestion at src/claudedeep/pipelines/clarification_gate.py. Policy defaults max_pipeline_recursion: int = 3, max_gap_iterations: int = 3, fast_path_enabled: bool = True, cache_ttl_seconds: int = 86400.

Part 3 — The substrate (retrieval, embeddings, graph, corpus)

Part 2 explained what happens when a Builder or Saboteur says “retrieve evidence.” Part 3 explains what that actually does. Every retrieval call passes through the same substrate: dense embeddings (bge-m3), sparse lexical (BM25), rank fusion (RRF), cross-encoder rerank (bge-reranker-v2-m3), graph traversal (FalkorDB + GLiNER NER), parent-document expansion, and trust-tier scoring.

3.0   The three retrieval query semantics

ClaudeDeep uses three semantically distinct retrieval modes, enforced by subtype. A Builder may only construct a SupportingQuery; a Saboteur only a CounterQuery; the Phase 2 proofing tier only an IntegrationQuery; the Master Orchestrator only an ArchitecturalQuery. The type system forbids the wrong caller from asking the wrong question — a Builder that accidentally issued a CounterQuery would ground its plan in anti-patterns, and the compiler prevents that at compile time.

QueryCallerSemantic domain
SupportingQueryBuilder (Phase 1)Best-practice implementations of module M
CounterQuerySaboteur (Phase 1)Anti-patterns, failure modes, wrong implementations
IntegrationQueryPhase 2 proofing tierBoundary patterns between two modules
ArchitecturalQueryMaster Orchestrator (Phase 0)High-level architectural patterns

3.1   CompiledQuery — the deterministic compiler

A raw QueryIntent from an LLM says “module=raft, intent=supporting, constraints=[strongly consistent, leader-elected].” It does not say “run this exact vector search string, then this exact Cypher pattern.” The compilation step turns semantic intent into deterministic, replayable, machine-executable queries: compile(intent) → CompiledQuery(vector_q, graph_pattern, filters). The compilation is pure — the same intent always compiles to the same query, with no LLM involved. This is what makes retrieval replayable: a telemetry event records the CompiledQuery, and any debugger can re-execute it later against the same substrate and get the same hits.

Verified against code. src/claudedeep/graphrag/query_dsl.py defines class QueryIntent and class CompiledQuery. class GraphRAGEngine at src/claudedeep/graphrag/engine.py exposes query_compiled(...) as the retrieval surface.

3.2   The GraphRAGEngine façade

GraphRAGEngine is the single entry point to retrieval. It owns a dense adapter, a graph adapter, and (optionally) a hybrid retriever. At construction it probes whether real backends are reachable and picks the real adapter over the in-memory fallback — the “no stub in default runtime” rule.

Verified against code. Real adapters: class RealLanceDBAdapter at src/claudedeep/graphrag/real_lancedb_adapter.py, class RealFalkorDBAdapter at src/claudedeep/graphrag/real_falkordb_adapter.py. In-memory fallbacks: class LanceDBAdapter at graphrag/lancedb_adapter.py, class FalkorDBAdapter at graphrag/falkordb_adapter.py. class GraphRAGHit and the four query classes at graphrag/queries.py.

3.3   Why bge-m3, LanceDB, BM25, RRF, and cross-encoder rerank

Dense embeddings: bge-m3

Three properties: 1024-dimensional embeddings (enough resolution for a large corpus without inflating the index); multilingual by design (the corpus is English-only today, but the model is ready for non-English CS references without a swap); long-context support up to 8192 tokens (so full parent-document chunks embed without truncation loss).

Why LanceDB over Qdrant / Milvus / FAISS / pgvector

LanceDB is embedded (no server process), persistent (WAL on-disk), supports incremental writes, and its columnar layout handles trust-layer filtering efficiently. Qdrant and Milvus require running services; FAISS lacks persistence semantics; pgvector requires Postgres. LanceDB wins on “no additional moving parts.”

Sparse + fusion: BM25 and RRF

Dense retrieval clusters by semantic similarity and can miss hits that share lexical tokens the model doesn’t consider close. BM25 (via rank_bm25.BM25Okapi) covers the lexical case. The two produce scores on incomparable scales, so ClaudeDeep fuses them with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: 

fused_score(chunk) = SUM over sources i of  1 / (k + rank_i(chunk))
                     k = 60  (Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009)

RRF is rank-based, so no normalization free-parameter is needed; it has diminishing returns; and it is robust to a chunk missing from one source.

Rerank: bge-reranker-v2-m3

Dense embeddings are bi-encoder (query and document encoded independently, a dot product for similarity) — fast but coarse. A cross-encoder concatenates [CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP] and runs one forward pass over the joint sequence, producing a scalar relevance logit that reflects true pairwise interaction. The right pattern: bi-encoder + BM25 to candidate, cross-encoder to rerank. The same bge-reranker-v2-m3 model serves double duty as the CrossEncoderPRM backend (Appendix B), so one download serves two purposes.

Verified against code. Env var CLAUDEDEEP_EMBED_MODEL selects the embedder; CLAUDEDEEP_NER_MODEL and CLAUDEDEEP_GLINER_MODEL select the NER model. class Reranker at src/claudedeep/pipelines/reranker.py. class TrustScorer at src/claudedeep/graphrag/trust_layer.py.

3.4   Parent-document chunking + graph store

Embeddings work best on small (~512-token) chunks; LLMs work best on large (~4096-token) chunks. Parent-document chunking resolves the tension: embed the 512-token child, but serve the 4096-token parent to the LLM. Each child stores a back-pointer to its parent.

The graph store answers relational queries dense retrieval cannot: “which chunks mention both Raft AND leader election?” FalkorDB is a Redis-backed, Cypher-compatible graph database. Entity extraction runs a fallback chain: GLiNER first, spaCy second, a capitalized-word heuristic last.

Verified against code. src/claudedeep/graphrag/ingestion.py holds the ingestion path. class ProvenanceRecord at src/claudedeep/graphrag/provenance.py. FalkorDB connection env vars CLAUDEDEEP_FALKORDB_HOST and CLAUDEDEEP_FALKORDB_PORT; LanceDB URI env var CLAUDEDEEP_LANCEDB_URI.

3.5   The trust layer

A chunk from a canonical textbook and a chunk from a random blog post can have similar cross-encoder logits, but they should not contribute equally. The trust layer re-scores every hit by tier × recency × corroboration before truncation.

TierContentsWeight
ACanonical textbooks, official docs, peer-reviewed papers, RFC/IEEE/ISO standards1.0
BWell-regarded conference papers, official OSS repos, authoritative technical books0.8
CUpvote-thresholded StackOverflow, community-vetted OSS, Wikipedia on technical topics0.5
provisionalFreshly ingested chunks from gap-resolver web search0.4
rejectedAI-generated content, editorially-uncontrolled blogs, marketing pages0.0 (never indexed)

Part 4 — The verifiers

The pipeline produces candidate answers. Part 4 decides whether they are worth trusting. Every quality signal — agreement-weighted voting, PRM scoring, tree-search selection, conformal-calibrated abstention — lives here.

4.0   The verifier stack — one call site, four factors

There is exactly one call site where the “how good is this candidate” question is asked: LLMStage._best_of_n() at src/claudedeep/pipelines/llm_stage.py:253. Four factors compose multiplicatively: 

final_confidence(winner) =
    agreement(winner)       # canonical clustering
  * prm_score(winner)       # Process Reward Model
  * subclaim_fraction       # sub-claim decomposition (Q.5)
  * ucb_selection_factor    # tree search, when engaged

Each factor is in [0, 1]. Any single factor going to zero collapses confidence to zero — ClaudeDeep would rather abstain than emit an answer that failed even one check.

4.1   PRM — five verifiers plus one router (Q-Fix.N)

Q-Fix.N refactored PRM dispatch from a single class into a typed family. The five reasons for separation reduce to: different verifiers have different training objectives, different hardware profiles, and different best-fit schemas.

ClassWhat it is
HeuristicPRMZero-dependency baseline: schema coverage × string density × structure. The fallback everything degrades to.
NoOpPRMAlways 1.0. Exercises the PRM code path without changing scores; for ablations.
CrossEncoderPRMWraps bge-reranker-v2-m3 (already cached for retrieval). One (prompt, output) logit, sigmoid to [0, 1]. Strong even before any trained PRM.
CodePRMScaffoldIntegration point for the real CodePRM (ACL 2025). Loads weights from CLAUDEDEEP_CODEPRM_WEIGHTS when present; otherwise delegates to CrossEncoderPRM.
GenerativeThinkPRMWraps launch/ThinkPRM-1.5B / 7B / 14B. A generative CoT verifier; parses per-step labels; score = correct / (correct + incorrect).
SchemaRoutedPRMTop-level router: code schemas → code PRM, reasoning schemas → ThinkPRM. The quality-max default.
Verified against code. All six classes exist in src/claudedeep/pipelines/prm.py: HeuristicPRM, NoOpPRM, CrossEncoderPRM, CodePRMScaffold, GenerativeThinkPRM, SchemaRoutedPRM, plus the ProcessRewardModel Protocol and legacy aliases CodePRMAdapter / ThinkPRMAdapter. Policy defaults: prm_kind: str = "auto" (i.e. HeuristicPRM by default; schema_routed only under quality-max), prm_reasoning_model: str = "launch/ThinkPRM-1.5B", prm_code_model: str = "BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3".

4.2   model_swap — the GPU pressure release valve

On a 4060 Ti 16 GB, gpt-oss:20b occupies ~13 GB, leaving no room to co-load a 1.5B–7B PRM. When prm_model_swap=True (the default), each score() call lazy-loads the PRM, scores, then releases it (del model + gc.collect() + torch.cuda.empty_cache()). Cost: 1–8 s of model load per call. On a datacenter GPU set it to False and the weights stay resident (~50–200 ms/call).

Verified against code. Policy fields prm_model_swap: bool = True and prm_device: Literal["auto", "cuda", "cpu"] = "auto" and prm_max_new_tokens: int = 1024. Env-var overrides CLAUDEDEEP_PRM_MODEL_SWAP, CLAUDEDEEP_PRM_DEVICE, CLAUDEDEEP_PRM_MAX_TOKENS.

4.3   The agreement fraction — canonical clustering

best-of-N produces N parsed Pydantic candidates. To pick a winner we cluster by canonical form (parsed.model_dump_json()) and count, not by embedding similarity. Canonical-form match guarantees that structurally-equivalent JSONs collide into one cluster and structurally- different answers never conflate. Agreement = winning-cluster-size / N.

4.4   Best-of-N, stratified sampling, and Tree-of-Thoughts

Under the quality-max overlay, best-of-N is stratified across the ensemble via round-robin, and the search strategy can switch from linear best-of-N to Tree-of-Thoughts with UCB1 expansion. UCB1 balances exploration and exploitation, preventing premature convergence on a single branch.

Reconciled against code (defaults). The code defaults are best_of_n: int = 5, search_strategy = "best_of_n", tree_branch_factor: int = 3, tree_depth: int = 2. The quality-max overlay raises these to 64 / tree / 4 / 3. The English book’s inline figures quoted the overlay values as if they were defaults; this edition states both.
Verified against code. class TreeSearch, class TreeSearchConfig, class TreeSearchResult at src/claudedeep/pipelines/tree_search.py. class MultiModelEnsemble, class EnsembleMember, class EnsembleResult at src/claudedeep/llm/ensemble.py. class SubClaimDecomposition, class SubClaimVerification, class Claim at src/claudedeep/pipelines/sub_claim.py.

4.5   Conformal calibration — making 99% precision a guarantee

The default abstention threshold is 0.85 — a folk-lore number nobody verified. Conformal prediction, given a held-out eval set of (confidence, was_correct) pairs, computes the smallest tau such that precision(conf ≥ tau) ≥ 1−ε, at a user-specified epsilon (default 0.01 for a 99% precision target). This is a distribution-free guarantee — no assumption about the confidence distribution’s shape. An empty calibration file preserves the heuristic 0.85 (the “never worsen the baseline” invariant).

Verified against code. class ConformalCalibrator, class CalibrationDatum, class CalibrationResult at src/claudedeep/pipelines/conformal.py. Policy fields conformal_calibration_path: str | None = None and conformal_epsilon: float = 0.01.

Part 5 — The failure recovery layer

Part 2 handles the happy path. Part 5 is what happens when the pipeline can’t answer. The principle: a wrong answer is worse than no answer. Before Phase 3 emits an AbstentionReport, ClaudeDeep exhausts three lines of recovery: online knowledge retrieval, an external verifier appeal, and formal proof.

5.1   Layer 1 — the Gap Resolver

When Phase 3 emits AbstentionReport(reason="corpus_gap") with a gap request, the outer loop invokes GapResolver.resolve(). The four stages: synthesize MCP-tool-typed queries (web_search, arxiv_search, github_search, paper_retrieval); retrieve chunks via the MCP handlers; screen each chunk through the ChunkSaboteur (single-pass) and, under quality-max, the MultiPassSaboteur (five families); ingest the survivors as provisional evidence. The outer loop then re-enters Phase 0 with the enriched corpus. At max_gap_iterations the abstention becomes final.

Verified against code. class GapResolver, class GapResolverResult, class GapDescriptor, class GapResolutionRequest at src/claudedeep/gap_resolver/. Four MCP handler files: web_search.py, arxiv_search.py, github_search.py, paper_retrieval.py under src/claudedeep/mcp/handlers/, plus a dispatcher.py. class McpRetriever and class StubMcpRetriever in the mcp package.

5.2   ChunkSaboteur and MultiPassSaboteur

The ChunkSaboteur is a single-pass gate against prompt-injection payloads, low-quality content, and known bad domains. Under quality-max the MultiPassSaboteur runs five independent attack families — injection, noise, duplicate (MinHash), bias, contradiction against tier-A sources — and requires that no family reject and the mean soft-score ≥ 0.65 for promotion. Rejected chunks are persisted as adversarial counter-examples for future Saboteur runs.

Verified against code. class ChunkSaboteur at src/claudedeep/gap_resolver/saboteur_screen.py; class MultiPassSaboteur, class MultiPassChunkSaboteur, class MultiPassResult at src/claudedeep/gap_resolver/multi_pass_saboteur.py. The five pass classes exist as NoisePass, BiasPass, DuplicatePass, ContradictionPass, and the injection pass, plus probe classes BiasProbe, ContradictionProbe, DuplicationProbe, QualityProbe, ChunkProbe.

5.3   Layer 2 — the cloud teacher

Before any corpus_gap abstention emits, Phase 3 consults the cloud teacher (gpt-oss:120b-cloud by default, temperature 0.0). The teacher returns a verdict: if it confirms the abstention, a tier-A “teacher-confirmed” evidence link is added and the abstention stands. If it proposes an alternative, the alternative is NEVER accepted directly — it re-enters Phase 1 as a SEED subject to the same Saboteur / PRM / SMT gates as any candidate. The teacher is a proposer, not a decider; even its answer must pass local verification, preserving the 100%-or-abstain invariant.

Verified against code. src/claudedeep/llm/cloud_teacher.py holds class CloudTeacherConfig and class CloudTeacherUnavailable. Policy fields cloud_teacher_model: str | None = None (i.e. off by default; gpt-oss:120b-cloud under quality-max) and cloud_teacher_timeout_s: float = 600.0.

5.4   Layer 3 — the Z3-SMT gate

For code-artifact answers with declared invariants (extracted from the contract’s api_schema), a final Z3 check runs. SAT: attach a positive evidence link. UNSAT: lower confidence by 0.2 and attach a human-readable UNSAT core; if the demoted confidence falls below tau, the answer becomes AbstentionReport(reason="unsat_core"). UNKNOWN (timeout): if the policy requires SMT, emit reason="proof_incomplete"; else attach a proof-timeout note and keep the answer.

Z3’s raw UNSAT core is a list of assertion IDs — useless to the user. The verifier maps each ID to its origin (which contract field, which module) and formats a readable summary such as: “Module A guarantees output.count ≥ 1 but Module B’s contract requires output.count = 0 — these are incompatible.” The user sees the WHY, not just the fact.

Part 7 — Trade-offs

Every mechanism was picked over alternatives. This part is the ledger, drawn from both books and pruned to only the decisions the code actually implements.

7.1   Per-mechanism trade-offs

Grammar-constrained decoding vs. free-form + post-parse

Buys: schema validity by construction, no retry loops. Costs: token-mask overhead; requires an inference server that supports it. Alternative: free-form generation + Pydantic post-parse + retry. Why this: retry loops break composability — a Builder that occasionally fails and retries produces non-deterministic latency, and best-of-N with retries has undefined semantics.

Canonical-form clustering vs. embedding similarity

Buys: exact-match semantics; structurally-identical answers collide, structurally-different answers never conflate. Costs: no fuzzy matching. Alternative: embed each candidate, cluster by cosine. Why this: two Plan candidates with different steps in the same order can embed close together but propose different plans; the agreement fraction must reflect real duplication, not semantic proximity.

Multiplicative confidence vs. additive

Buys: any weakness is fatal; a high-agreement, low-PRM answer cannot beat a low-agreement, high-PRM one. Costs: a single low factor tanks the whole score. Alternative: weighted sum. Why this: a model can be very consistent about a wrong answer; agreement and quality are orthogonal and both must be high.

Deterministic-arbiters cascade vs. LLM judge

Buys: no override cascade; the confidence chain stays traceable. Costs: more code paths (six tiers vs. one judge). Alternative: a single LLM judge that reads and patches conflicting contracts. Why this: the LLM judge is exactly the override cascade Gap 2 warned about; once an ungrounded LLM overwrites peer decisions, auditability is gone.

Explicitly rejected: multi-agent debate as the conflict resolver. Debate systems, used to resolve module contracts, produce over-confident consensus on wrong answers — the agreement of two adversarial LLMs is evidence that they agree, not that they are right. Deterministic arbiters avoid this by construction. This is the central design principle: don’t make one model responsible for proving its own correctness.

7.2   Overall trade-offs

AxisClaudeDeep’s choiceThe cost
Quality vs. latencyQuality first; no latency budgetMinutes to hours per query under quality-max
Coverage vs. precisionPrecision first (99% on answered)35–55% answer rate on Verified; the rest abstain
Open-weight vs. cloud frontierOpen-weight 7B–20B primary + cloud teacher on appealAbsolute pass-rate ceiling below the frontier
Complexity vs. simplicityHigh architectural complexity, held simple by type-level invariantsA steep learning curve (hence this book)
No-stub-in-default (Q-Fix.A)Real backends by default; stubs are test-onlyFirst run needs models + corpus + Ollama present

  • Five PRM classes + SchemaRoutedPRM router, byte-identical across all four mode folders.
  • Seven new policy fields (prm_kind, prm_code_model, prm_reasoning_model, prm_codeprm_weights, prm_model_swap, prm_device, prm_max_new_tokens), seven env-var overrides, seven CLI flags.
  • launch/ThinkPRM-1.5B (~3.4 GB) and launch/ThinkPRM-7B (~14 GB) downloaded from Hugging Face.
  • Integration test test_prm_q_fix_n.py: 21/21 pass.

8.4   SWE-bench subset (honest result)

Result, stated plainly. A 3-instance SWE-bench Verified subset ran on the astropy instances and produced 0/3 patches, all three hitting the 1200-second per-instance timeout, and the run executed in --mode baseline (single-shot gpt-oss:20b), NOT the full pipeline. The full-pipeline subset re-run with a realistic timeout is deferred to an overnight session. The 500-instance benchmark has not been run. There is no committed SWE-bench score.

8.6   What we explicitly DO NOT claim

Not Mythos-parity on raw pass-rate. Mythos sits at 93.9%. The realistic first-year outcome for a 7B–20B-class model with the full stack is 35–55% on Verified. The gap is structural (model size + training data + alignment) and no test-time scaffolding closes it on current published evidence. The claim is precision-on-answered parity at lower coverage, not raw pass-rate.
No committed benchmark number today. See 8.4.
No conformal-calibration eval set in the repo. The ConformalCalibrator code is exercised by property tests, but no real (confidence, was_correct) JSON has been harvested. The 99% precision floor is designed-in, not yet measured-in; default behavior reverts to the heuristic 0.85.
No real CodePRM weights loaded by default. The ACL 2025 CodePRM authors have not publicly released weights. CodePRMScaffold loads from CLAUDEDEEP_CODEPRM_WEIGHTS when the user provides them; otherwise it delegates to CrossEncoderPRM (bge-reranker-v2-m3).

Appendix B — How logits are used across ClaudeDeep

The organizing principle: every logit either flows into an argmax (token generation) or into a sigmoid (a scalar quality score); nowhere else. Understanding those two paths in full covers 100% of logit usage in the codebase.

B.0   What a logit is

A logit is the raw, pre-activation output of a network’s final linear layer, before softmax or sigmoid. It lives in (−∞, +∞). Two flavors appear: a single-scalar logit from a regression head (sigmoid gives a probability), and a token-distribution logit vector at each generation step (softmax gives the next-token distribution).

B.1   The six entry points

B.1.1   gpt-oss:20b token generation (constrained-decoded)

The model computes token logits at each step; Ollama’s format=json-schema masks any token that would break the JSON to −∞ before sampling. ClaudeDeep never reads these logits directly — it reads the sampled tokens as a validated Pydantic instance. This is what makes the LLM-as-syntax-compiler invariant a hard runtime guarantee. Temperature: 0.7 for best-of-N diversity, 0.9 at ToT root, 0.0 for the cloud teacher.

B.1.2   bge-reranker-v2-m3 — the CrossEncoderPRM path

The cross-encoder emits one scalar logit r for a [CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP] pair. We compose query = system_prompt + user_content, passage = parsed.model_dump_json(), then score = 1 / (1 + exp(-r)). The reranker was trained on relevance, not correctness, so this is a strong approximation, not a calibrated correctness estimator. Sigmoid, not softmax, because a single logit has no second dimension to normalize against, and σ(0)=0.5 gives a natural neutral midpoint.

B.1.3   CodePRMScaffold — regression head

Same shape as B.1.2 but loaded as AutoModelForSequenceClassification. Forward pass produces logits.shape = (1, 1); we take the scalar and sigmoid. Different weights (calibrated to code correctness), identical downstream. Dormant on default installs until CLAUDEDEEP_CODEPRM_WEIGHTS is set.

B.1.4   GenerativeThinkPRM — implicit logit consumption via greedy argmax

ThinkPRM is a causal LM with no regression head. We call model.generate(do_sample=False, temperature=0.0), which picks argmax over next-token logits at each step. Logits are consumed internally; we never see them. We parse the generated critique text for \boxed{correct|incorrect} and “step N is (correct|incorrect)” labels and aggregate: score = correct / (correct + incorrect); 0.5 if no labels parse. Fraction, not sigmoid, because the per-step labels are already calibrated. Greedy, not sampling, because a verifier must be a function of its input.

B.1.5   GLiNER NER — graph ingestion only

GLiNER emits per-span classification logits; sigmoid → probability; threshold 0.5 accepts an entity. Used only to MERGE (:Chunk)-[:MENTIONS]->(:Entity) edges into FalkorDB. No interaction with the LLMStage confidence path.

B.1.6   gpt-oss:120b-cloud teacher

Same constrained-decoding path as B.1.1, larger backend, temperature 0.0. We read the sampled tokens as a TeacherVerdict; never see the logits.

B.2   Where logits are deliberately not read

  • Best-of-N clustering uses canonical-form match, not logit or embedding similarity.
  • Sub-claim verification reads GraphRAG hits, not logits.
  • Conformal calibration operates on already-computed confidence, not logits.

B.3   The full flow

LLMStage.run()
  -> best_of_N (N=64 under quality-max)
       B.1.1 OllamaConstrainedDecoder: token logits -> JSON-schema mask -> parsed Pydantic
  -> canonical clustering: key = model_dump_json(); agreement = |winner| / N
  -> PRM.score(winner):
       B.1.2 CrossEncoderPRM: r -> sigmoid
       B.1.3 CodePRMScaffold: r -> sigmoid
       B.1.4 GenerativeThinkPRM: generate (argmax) -> parse -> fraction
       HeuristicPRM: no logits
  -> combined = agreement * score
  -> LLMResult(parsed, confidence=combined, evidence)
  -> Phase 3: if combined >= tau -> AnswerReport; else cloud teacher / SMT / AbstentionReport

Appendix D — Independent architectural assessment

Provenance note. What follows is adapted from an independent assessment of this architecture’s design lineage, originally written in the CAM manuscript against the working name “Cyrbra Ather Mind.” It is reproduced here condensed to its distinct substantive content. It is an assessment of the design, not a claim about measured performance — see Part 8 for the empirical state.

D.1   The central claim

ClaudeDeep does not attempt to make a mid-tier model behave like a frontier model in a single pass; it builds a reasoning environment that enables a mid-tier model to construct, attack its own construction, use evidence, detect failure, rebuild, verify, and integrate results — until the system arrives at a defensible outcome.

D.2   The fundamental idea

Reasoning does not all have to live inside the model’s weights. Take a strong-enough self-hosted model and use it as a reasoning substrate, while the architecture around it supplies task decomposition, reasoning policies, knowledge grounding, adversarial challenge, counter-evidence, error discovery, verification, correction, integration, and the final decision.

D.3   The primary model need not be frontier-class

The threshold is not “is it the smartest model in the world?” but: does it understand, focus reasonably, follow a Skill, emit JSON, call functions, read evidence, and revise itself? If those hold at a decent level, the architecture can do a great deal of work on top.

D.5   Two forms of externalized memory

Knowledge memory (what is known, from corpus + graph) and failure memory (what could go wrong, from FAQs + failure patterns). Together they produce something stronger than plain retrieval: the system retrieves facts and the map of the places where those facts get misapplied.

D.6   The adversarial primitive

The Saboteur is not there to say “I disagree.” It is there to say “try to prove this candidate is wrong.” The Builder asks “how do I construct a good solution?”; the Saboteur asks “how do I break it?” That is adversarial verification, not debate.

D.10   Where the leverage comes from — the loop

The primary model may produce an imperfect first attempt. ClaudeDeep is not obliged to accept it: First Attempt → Counter Evidence → Saboteur Attack → Failure → Failure Analysis → Rebuild → Attack Again → Verify. You are not asking for perfect first-pass reasoning; you are building iterative reasoning + error correction.

D.12   The economics this creates

Instead of “pay for a stronger frontier model to do everything,” it becomes “use a locally-capable model, and build an architecture around it that gives it knowledge, prescribes its reasoning procedure, attacks it, detects its errors, corrects it, and verifies it.” The developer’s trade: less money + more independence + offline + data control, in exchange for higher latency + larger local compute.

D.14   The most important sentence

Don’t make one model responsible for proving its own correctness. This architectural principle generalizes to any reasoning system. Any system that violates it — a single frontier model, or a multi-agent debate without deterministic arbiters — will produce over-confident consensus on wrong answers.

ClaudeDeep as an architectural concept: a defensible 9-to-9.5/10 design. Not because every technology in it is new, but because it attempts something deeper — making reasoning a property of the whole system, not a property exclusive to the model. Whether that design delivers operationally depends on the substrate work Part 8 lays out honestly; the design itself is the contribution.
